figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Matrix-Game 4.0. From top: the system loop; diagonal split-screen comparisons between low-poly engine outputs and neural renderings on held-out validation examples; gameplay examples from games created by the coding agent in response to user requests; end-to-end latency comparisons with recent systems (Table 3) and the rendering throughput at 480p on a single RTX 5090.
figures.headline: Split-screen comparisons show neural renderings adding materials and lighting while keeping the layout of the low-poly engine output.
citing_sentences: In the resulting proxy the sky is black and the ground is a gray checkerboard; buildings and walls become flat-colored boxes and prisms, trees become a cylinder with a sphere, characters become figures made of blocks, and every primitive is drawn with a black outline and no texture, reflection, or shadow (left part of each split frame in Figure 1).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Roadmap of Matrix-Game V4: The multimodal coding agent and the game engine form the harness for the video generation model. The player sends ideas and requests to the agent and actions to the engine (1). The agent writes the world, turning ideas into game code and scenes for the engine, and translates the world, turning the state and events reported by the engine into text descriptions. The engine maintains the world state and the rules in code (2) and sends control signals as a structural rendering of the scene (3). The video generation model renders frames in real time from the text description, its past frames, and the structural rendering (4). The generated frame returns to the player as visual feedback (5).
figures.headline: The roadmap diagram shows player input, agent code, engine state and video frames passing through a loop from action to visual feedback.
citing_sentences: Figure 2 shows how the three parts work together.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: UE5 paired training data. (a) Each clip is captured twice in Unreal Engine 5 under the same camera and frame index: once as a low-poly structure render (BBox) that preserves scene layout and motion, and once as the high-fidelity RGB frame. (b) For every 81-frame clip, frame-aligned CSV records of camera pose, actions, visible objects, events, and environment are turned into a prompt: visible object IDs are looked up in a description table, spatial and temporal cues are composed, and a template produces the clip prompt.
figures.headline: Low-poly and high-fidelity frames are pixel-aligned, and each training prompt is assembled from engine object states and events.
citing_sentences: Camera trajectories and timestamps are strictly synchronized between the two renders, so the low-poly structure frame and the high-fidelity frame of the same index are aligned pixel by pixel (Figure 3a).

The system reads the currently visible objects and their real-time states from the game engine and fills them into a prompt template, producing a description that matches the current frame (Figure 3b).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Dynamic captions follow the engine state. Top: low-poly proxy frames of one CitySample driving clip; numbered markers are the visible objects that the engine reports for this frame, each linked by its instance ID to a semantic description. Below: the caption that the rule-based template produces for the same frame, without any vision-language model. Orange text comes from object states and events, and blue text from object positions and distances. As the car moves, parked vehicles leave the description, pedestrians change from standing to approaching, and newly visible objects are announced under “Changes”.
figures.headline: Dynamic captions change as the car moves, removing parked vehicles and updating pedestrian states from engine reports.
citing_sentences: When the player changes the view, enters a new area, or triggers an event, the description is reorganized, so the video model always receives the latest semantic condition (Figure 4).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Architecture of the rendering model. The noisy latent of one chunk (one latent frame, four video frames) and the low-poly proxy encoded by TAEHV are concatenated into 148 channels and patchified into 405 tokens per latent frame at $480\times 864$. Thirty causal DiT blocks apply self-attention over a KV cache that holds spatial-memory frames, reference frames, and the latest 20 chunks, cross-attention to the cached text keys and values of the dynamic caption, and a feed-forward network, each modulated by the timestep through AdaLN. The output head predicts a velocity, one or two flow updates produce the clean latent, and TAEHV decodes four frames. The finished chunk is then re-run at $t=0$ without the control input to write its keys and values into the cache.
figures.headline: The rendering network concatenates the proxy with the noisy latent and passes it through causal attention blocks with a KV cache.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 shows the network, whose DiT has 5B parameters.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Overview of the inference optimizations. (a) Per-block GPU time on an RTX 5090, broken down by kernel category. (b) Decoding is moved ahead of the clean-KV update, so frames are output earlier. (c) Instead of shifting the whole KV window at every step, the ring cache writes the new frame into the oldest slot. (d) Self-attention is split into seven window ranges whose quantized keys and values are cached; the partial outputs are combined by log-sum-exp.
figures.headline: Per-block timing and three cache and decoding changes are shown, each reducing waiting on the GPU during inference.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Re-rendering over 40-second held-out rollouts. For each game, the upper row is the low-poly proxy from the engine and the lower row is the frame generated by the distilled causal model at the same time step. The generated frames follow the proxy layout, camera, and object motion throughout the rollout, while the model fills in materials, vegetation, lighting, smoke, and muzzle effects.
figures.headline: Rollouts over 40 seconds keep the proxy layout, camera path and object motion while adding materials, lighting and effects.
citing_sentences: Figure 7 shows three held-out rollouts at four time steps.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Game modes written with the coding agent, rendered in real time. Top: in the third-person shooter, the agent adds health and ammunition control, shield durability, a faster shotgun, a game-over condition, and simple sound effects. Middle: in the driving game, the agent implements a time trial with route checkpoints and collision penalties. Bottom: the same driving game turned into a pursuit mode, in which the player must intercept a target vehicle and stay close to it for five seconds. The engine evaluates every rule; the video model renders each frame from the engine output.
figures.headline: Three game modes written by the coding agent run in real time, with the engine enforcing rules and the video model rendering each frame.
citing_sentences: Figure 8 shows three modes built this way.

abstract: Moving from controllable videos to genuinely playable worlds requires persistent world state, executable game rules, and low-latency interaction. We outline a roadmap for the next generation of Matrix-Game that separates game execution from visual generation through an executable game harness, and introduce Matrix-Game 4.0 as the first system built on this design. A lightweight game engine maintains world state and executes interaction rules, a multimodal coding agent translates player ideas into game code and dynamic scene captions, and a renderer based on autoregressive video model transforms engine-rendered low-poly proxies into detailed visuals, conditioned on dynamic captions and memory references. This framework provides continuous guidance for visual generation and enables natural-language creation and modification of scenes and gameplay. Our renderer is trained on aligned low-poly and high-fidelity video pairs and distilled into a causal generator that generates in four-frame chunks with one or two denoising steps. Together with targeted inference optimizations, Matrix-Game 4.0 enables 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090 with a key-press-to-display latency of 112 ms. Single-step generation achieves 83 FPS steady-state throughput with 18.2 GiB of peak GPU memory usage. With fixed prompts, steady-state throughput also reaches 67 FPS on an RTX 5080 and 58 FPS on an RTX 5070 Ti. We demonstrate customizable shooter and driving games with engine-enforced mechanics, and release code, model weights, and low-poly game assets to support research and creation of playable game worlds.

sections.body: The introduction argues that video-only world models struggle with persistent state, error accumulation, memory that grows with rollout length, and limited gameplay rules. It argues that diffusion models learn statistical correlations and that current video generators act mostly as renderers. The authors propose placing a video generation model in an external harness that holds world state and rules, with a multimodal coding agent that writes game code. The listed contributions are real-time 480p gameplay on a single RTX 5090 at 112 ms latency, a roadmap, a reusable pipeline, and an open-source release. Figure 1 and Figure 2 summarize the system.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Playable worlds need persistent state, executable rules and low latency, which motivates separating game logic from video generation.

sections.body: The roadmap wraps a video model in a harness with three modules. The game engine acts as referee: it keeps state for health, inventory, gravity, collisions and quest progress, and it outputs structural renderings that constrain layout, object motion and camera viewpoint. The multimodal coding agent turns player ideas into game code and scene edits, and it converts engine events into text descriptions for the video model. The video model autoregressively generates short sequences of future frames from these descriptions, past frames and structural renderings. The section gives no quantitative evaluation and describes the design and the intended role of each module.
sections.heading: Roadmap
sections.headline: A game engine, a coding agent and a video model form a harness, with the engine holding world state and enforcing rules.

sections.body: The authors build a dataset in Unreal Engine 5 covering a medieval castle, an ancient Egypt desert, desert canyon air combat, and the CitySample megacity. Each capture yields pixel-aligned low-poly and high-fidelity videos at 1280 by 720, a depth render, and per-frame metadata. Table 1 lists 114,334 training clips totaling 1,712 hours, and held-out capture sessions contribute no training clips. The low-poly proxy keeps spatial topology, rigid poses and motion trajectories, and removes textures, reflections and complex lighting. Dynamic captions are produced by a rule-based template from visible object IDs and their states, without a vision-language model.
sections.heading: Data
sections.headline: Paired Unreal Engine captures of low-poly and high-fidelity video give 114,334 training clips across four scene types.

sections.body: The renderer starts from Wan2.2 Fun Control weights and becomes a video-to-video model with a DiT of 5B parameters. Four inputs condition each chunk: the proxy concatenated with the noisy latent, the dynamic caption, spatial-memory reference frames, and the first frame. Fine-tuning uses 81-frame windows at 704 by 1280 pixels for 4,000 steps. Distillation has three stages: teacher-forced causal training, causal consistency distillation, and asymmetric distribution matching. The final student denoises each chunk in one or two steps, and its KV cache holds three spatial-memory frames, reference frames and the latest 20 chunks. The section reports no quality metric for the distilled model.
sections.heading: Rendering Model
sections.headline: A video model is distilled into a causal generator that denoises each four-frame chunk in one or two steps.

sections.body: Table 2 adds optimizations one at a time on one RTX 5090 at 480 by 864. The changes include the TAEHV decoder, a fused RoPE kernel with cached text keys and values, 8-bit weights with a CUDA Graph, one-step distillation, an asynchronous I/O pipeline, fused Triton kernels, a ring KV cache, and split-KV FlashAttention. The overall result is 19× faster throughput and 9.9× lower latency. Measured on the model alone, throughput is about 83 FPS with one step and about 57 FPS with two, with about 18.2 GiB peak memory. With fixed prompts on 16 GiB cards, throughput is about 67 FPS on an RTX 5080 and 58 FPS on an RTX 5070 Ti.
sections.heading: Real-Time Inference
sections.headline: Cumulative optimizations raise steady-state throughput from 4.5 to 83.4 FPS and cut latency from 1110 ms to 112 ms.

sections.body: The setup uses one rendering model per game and held-out rollouts of 961 frames, which is 40 seconds at 24 FPS, at 480 by 864. Qualitative results show that generated frames keep the proxy layout and camera path, add stone walls, palm trees and smoke, and keep the character's appearance across the rollout. Table 3 compares latency and openness with Code World Model, StreamRender-H3, AgentGarten and Magpie. Matrix-Game 4.0 reports 112 ms, the lowest latency in the table, and it is the only system listed that runs on a single consumer GPU. The section gives no quantitative visual-quality metric, and the gameplay customization is shown only through examples.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: Visual results are qualitative only, but Matrix-Game 4.0 reports the lowest latency among four compared systems.

sections.body: Related work covers interactive video world models such as Genie, GameNGen, DIAMOND, Oasis and Matrix-Game 2.0 and 3.0, where the network carries both world dynamics and visuals. A second group, including Code World Model, Programmable World Model, StreamRender-H3, AgentGarten and Magpie, assigns state and rules to code and renders with a video model. The section also covers neural rendering and structure-conditioned generation, and real-time autoregressive generation with methods such as DMD, CausVid and Causal Forcing++. The authors place Matrix-Game 4.0 in the second group and note that its coding agent edits rules and writes prompts during play.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior interactive models keep dynamics in the network, while several recent systems assign rules to code and render with video.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the separation of game execution from visual generation: the engine runs rules and state, and the video model generates visuals. It reports 83 FPS steady-state throughput at 480p with one denoising step and 112 ms key-press-to-display latency in the evaluated configuration. Future work targets lower inference cost and hardware requirements, with a stated goal of a technical preview on Steam. Other directions include visual fidelity, a refinement stage for higher-resolution output, multiplayer rendering with consistent views across players, more precise control of visuals, and additional game genres and scenes.
sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
sections.headline: The harness design is offered as a reusable foundation, with lower inference cost and hardware needs left as near-term work.
